lessons.title: Market Impact: How Your Own Order Moves the Price

children.text: Lesson 1 covered spread cost, a fixed tax on every trade regardless of size. Market impact is the opposite: it does not exist at small size, and grows the moment your order is larger than what is quietly resting at the best bid or best ask. It was also the single largest component in Chapter 1's case study, responsible for 40% of the gap between a 22.4% backtest and a 4.1% live result. This lesson explains exactly why.

The best ask is only good for however many shares are actually sitting there. Beyond that quantity, a market order has to fill against the next price level, then the next, each one worse than the last. This is called walking the book. Consider a stock with the following resting sell orders.

body.caption: Ask-side order book for a mid-cap stock

children.text: A market order to buy 3,000 shares consumes all 500 at ₹250.00, all 800 at ₹250.10, all 1,200 at ₹250.25, and the remaining 500 at ₹250.40. The average fill price across the whole order works out to ₹250.19, roughly 0.08% above the best ask, even though not a single share traded above ₹250.40. A backtest that assumes this entire order fills at ₹250.00, the quoted price, has quietly understated the true cost by that 0.08%, on top of whatever spread cost Lesson 1 already accounted for.

children.text: The Square-Root Law: How Impact Scales With Order Size

markDefs.definition: An order's size expressed as a share of average daily traded value, e.g. an order worth 5% of ADV has a 5% participation rate.

children.text: Walking the book by hand only works when you have the actual order book. For backtesting, quant researchers rely on an empirical relationship observed across most liquid markets, including Indian equities: market impact grows with the square root of

body.caption: I: market impact as a percentage of trade value. k: an empirical constant (commonly around 0.5 for Indian equities, calibrate per market). σ: the stock's daily volatility (%). Q: order value. ADV: average daily traded value.

body.title: Market Impact vs Participation Rate (k = 0.5, σ = 2%)

children.text: Read the curve carefully: going from 1% to 25% of ADV, a 25 times larger order, only increases impact 5 times, from 0.10% to 0.50%, because impact scales with the square root of size, not size itself. This sub-linear relationship is exactly why large funds slice big orders into smaller pieces over time, spreading a trade across many small participation rates costs far less in total than executing it all at once at one large participation rate.
Worked Example: Buying ₹50 Lakh of a Midcap Stock
Take a midcap stock with ₹8 crore average daily traded value and 2% daily volatility, using the same k = 0.5. A ₹50 lakh order is 6.25% of ADV.

children.text: Why End-of-Day Backtests Miss This Entirely

A backtest built on daily closing prices has no order book at all, only a single number per stock per day. It cannot distinguish between a strategy trading ₹50,000 and one trading ₹50 lakh, both simply fill at the same closing price. Chapter 1's case study showed exactly what this blind spot costs: market impact alone accounted for 7.4 of the 18.3 percentage points separating a 22.4% backtest from a 4.1% live result, more than transaction costs and spread slippage combined.

body.text: Market impact cannot be sized correctly without knowing the average daily traded value of every stock a strategy trades, at the time it trades, not just at the end of the backtest. A strategy that looks size-agnostic in a backtest almost certainly is not size-agnostic once you check ADV against intended order size, stock by stock.

children.text: Coding a Simple Square-Root Impact Model

body.caption: Square-root market impact, ready to plug into a backtest
body.code:
import math

def market_impact_pct(order_value, adv, daily_vol_pct, k=0.5):
    """Estimated one-way market impact, as a percentage of order value.
    order_value, adv: same currency units (e.g. both in rupees).
    daily_vol_pct: daily volatility, e.g. 2.0 for 2%.
    """
    participation = order_value / adv
    return k * daily_vol_pct * math.sqrt(participation)

# Reproduces the worked example above
impact = market_impact_pct(order_value=5000000, adv=80000000, daily_vol_pct=2.0)
print(round(impact, 2))  # 0.25

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Using the square-root law, if an order's participation rate quadruples (for example from 4% to 16% of ADV), what happens to its estimated market impact?
body.explanation: Impact scales with the square root of participation rate. The square root of a 4x increase is 2x, so impact roughly doubles, not quadruples. This is exactly what the chart in this lesson shows: 4% participation gave 0.20% impact, and 16% participation gave 0.40% impact.

body.text: Market impact does not exist for a small order and grows with the square root of order size relative to average daily traded value for a large one. A backtest that fills every trade at the quoted or closing price, with no reference to ADV, cannot see this at all, and it is usually the single largest hidden cost once a strategy trades real size.

points: Market impact comes from walking the order book: once an order exceeds what is resting at the best price, later shares fill at progressively worse prices, raising the average fill price above the quoted price.
Impact scales with the square root of participation rate (order value divided by ADV), not linearly, so a 4x larger order produces roughly 2x, not 4x, the impact.
A ₹50 lakh order against ₹8 crore ADV, a 6.25% participation rate, produced an estimated 0.25% one-way and 0.50% round-trip impact in this lesson's worked example.

End-of-day, closing-price backtests cannot see market impact at all, since they have no order book and no concept of order size relative to liquidity, which is exactly why it was the largest single cost component in Chapter 1's case study.
